title-group.article-title: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism following haematopoietic stem cell transplant for multiple sclerosis in an adult female: a case report and literature review

sec.title: Summary
sec.p: Haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is a novel treatment utilised in a number of malignant and non-malignant conditions, with promising results in multiple sclerosis (MS), particularly in those not responding to previous disease-modifying therapies. There is existing evidence to suggest that HSCT has been linked to, in rare cases, autoimmune thyroid dysfunction. Much of the current literature highlights paediatric occurrences. The most common dysfunction noted is hypothyroidism, seen in 40% of cases, with other autoimmune thyroid dysfunctions reported less commonly. A 34-year-old female represents a unique case of autoimmune hyperthyroidism secondary to haematopoietic stem cell transplant completed for relapsing-remitting MS. One year following her HSCT, she presented with fatigue, brain fog, palpitations and tremors, and blood tests revealed thyrotoxicosis with elevated thyroid receptor antibody levels (TSH receptor antibodies). She was diagnosed with Graves’ disease and treated with carbimazole and propranolol acutely; she is currently under regular endocrine follow-up. Ongoing multidisciplinary collaboration to holistically support her complex health needs continues, and a symptomatic improvement has been noted.

list-item.p: Secondary autoimmune diseases, such as Graves’ disease, can develop in 2–14% of patients following autologous HSCT for MS.
In our case, the timeline for development of Graves’ disease post-HSCT is 10–12 months, which aligns with a previous reported case in the literature of between 8 and 32 months.
Thyroid function test should be monitored regularly post-HSCT for MS as both autoimmune hyperthyroidism (Graves’ disease) and hypothyroidism can develop.
We aim to highlight to clinicians about this rare occurrence of Graves’ disease post-HSCT.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Haematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) represents a key therapeutic option for disease modification in numerous conditions, both neoplastic and otherwise (1, 2). However, delayed-onset morbidities following the use of HSCT are becoming ever increasingly recognised as complications (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). These include thyroid dysfunction, with evidence suggesting autoimmune hypothyroidism as the most common manifestation (1, 2, 3, 4, 6).

HSCT resets the immune system through ablation of autoreactive lymphocytes and reconstitution with new haematopoietic stem cells. However, this process can create immune dysregulation, primarily due to a delayed recovery of T cell regulatory function and a relatively faster recovery of B cells, resulting in autoimmune hyperthyroidism (7).
This case represents a unique occurrence of autoimmune hyperthyroidism (Graves’ disease) secondary to autologous HSCT for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) in an adult female.

sec.title: Case presentation
sec.p: A 34-year-old female presented to her general practitioner with a history of acute-onset fatigue, general malaise, difficulty concentrating, palpitations, hot flushes and tremors. Thyroid function tests (TFTs) revealed a grossly elevated T4 and suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) (T4 = 50.8 pmol/L, range: 11–22 pmol/L; TSH < 0.01 mu/L, range: 0.27–4.2 mU/L). She was referred urgently to her local secondary care endocrinology team.

On examination, there was no goitre, normal eye examination and no cervical lymph nodes. There was noted to be a mild tremor in both hands. Her weight was 78.3 kg, with reassuringly normal observations (heart rate: 90 bpm, blood pressure: 135/88, oxygen saturation: 99% in air, and normothermic).

Thyroid antibody tests revealed a raised thyroid receptor antibody (TRAB), and a diagnosis of Graves’ disease was therefore made. Treatment with carbimazole 30 mg daily and propranolol 40 mg three times a day was initiated.

She was well known to a tertiary neurology team, with a background of relapsing-remitting MS. The first symptoms commenced at the age of 20 years, and she had undergone numerous trials of disease-modifying medications, including glatiramer (utilised in 2012, stopped due to intolerance) and natalizumab (utilised between 2012 and 2022).

One year prior to presentation (March 2023), she underwent an autologous HSCT with a stem cell dose of 9.1 × 106 CD34/kg. The conditioning regimen included cyclophosphamide and antithymocyte globulin (ATG). Her treatment was complicated by neutropenic sepsis and deranged liver function test post-ATG, as well as a new acute biventricular failure with functional tricuspid and mitral regurgitation and acute pericardial effusion. She remains under the care of a tertiary cardiology team to support her recovery.
Ten months prior to presentation (two months following HSCT), it was noted that she was experiencing deteriorating long-distance visual acuity and bilateral intermittent tinnitus.
Further past medical history included HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets) syndrome during a pregnancy and psoriasis.
Social history revealed that she drinks alcohol occasionally but does not take recreational drugs. She does smoke about 3–5 tobacco cigarettes a day.
Medications on presentation to general practitioner included lansoprazole 30 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily and eplerenone 25 mg daily.

sec.title: Investigation
sec.p: On presentation, she had a free T4 level of 50.8 (11–22pmol/L), TSH of < 0.01 (0.27–4.2 mU/L), a TRAB level of 26 (0–3.3 iU/L)) and normal TPO levels. Her T4, TSH and TRAB levels were regularly monitored for titration of carbimazole. sec.p: Other laboratory results were measured on presentation, including full blood count, renal function, haematinics and vitamin B12/folate levels. These revealed nil of acute concern.
The patient received ongoing investigations from her tertiary neurology team in regard to her MS.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: On initial presentation, she was treated with carbimazole 30 mg daily and propranolol 40 mg three times daily, with a review of blood tests six to eight weeks following. She was also given propranolol 40 mg three times daily. Smoking cessation was advised. Her carbimazole dose was regularly titrated in response to T4 and TSH levels listed Table 1 and symptomatic changes. Management of her thyrotoxicosis proved challenging, with even minor dose adjustments resulting in recurrence of her thyrotoxic symptoms. Due to her fluctuating symptoms of both hyperthyroidism – including palpitations, mood swings and irritability – and hypothyroidism – such as fatigue, cold intolerance and a flare of her MS symptoms (Lhermitte’s phenomenon) – a block and replace regime was initiated for her Graves’ disease with inclusion of levothyroxine of 100 micrograms once daily. She remained under ongoing endocrinology follow-up with future plans to discuss possibility of definitive treatment options, including total thyroidectomy, due to challenges in achieving optimal control of her Graves’ disease with the current medical therapy.

sec.title: Outcome and follow-up
sec.p: As part of her regular follow-up with the endocrinology, neurology and cardiology teams involved in her case, this patient has six-to-eight weekly blood tests monitoring TFTs, regular face-to-face endocrinology clinic appointments, telephone appointments with her neurology team (including MS clinical nurse specialist) and telephone appointments with her cardiology team. Further discussion between the MDT and patient will take place to consider the utility of a thyroidectomy if current medical therapy remains variably successful in controlling her thyrotoxic symptoms and TFTs.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This distinctive case of HSCT-induced Graves’ thyrotoxicosis on the background of relapsing-remitting MS in an adult female provides insight for clinicians into the essential nature of TFT monitoring post-HSCT.

Autologous HSCT for MS is associated with development of secondary autoimmune diseases (2ndADs), particularly immune thrombocytopenic purpura, hypothyroidism, or hyperthyroidism in the form of Graves’ disease (2). This is due to dysfunctional or imbalanced rebuilding of immune system post-HSCT affecting T-cells with delayed thymic re-education that can lead to development of autoimmunity. There is some suggestion of adoptive immunity transfer contributing to the development of thyroid dysfunction in paediatric case reports (7), but the thyroid status of the donor for this patient is unknown. Whilst not shown to be statistically significant, a multicentre retrospective study found a trend towards younger patients (<34.7 years old) exhibiting a greater risk of development of 2ndADs (8). The use of ATG within the conditioning regimen has been suggested to be associated with the development of a 2ndAD, when combined with ex vivo CD34-positive selection post-peripheral blood stem cell mobilisation (8). This study, however, does not isolate risk factors associated with the development of Graves’ disease specifically.

In a large observational prospective study, data of 507 patients who underwent HSCT for MS over 16 years showed that 3.3% developed hyperthyroidism/Graves’ disease. The mean time was 3.6 years following the treatment with a range of one to nine years (2). In this case, the patient developed clinical and biochemical features of Graves’ disease around a year after she had HSCT, which aligns with previously reported cases.

It is essential to distinguish autoimmune conditions induced by HSCT from those that may arise as a result of disease-modifying therapies. This patient was treated with a disease-modifying medication, natalizumab, which has been linked to rare case reports of thyroiditis rather than Graves’ disease. This is unlike alemtuzumab, which is commonly known to cause this associated with thyroid complications (9, 10). She then had a non-alemtuzumab-based autologous HSCT regimen with cyclophosphamide and ATG (antithymocyte globulin). It is for this reason that multidisciplinary professionals felt that her disease-modifying medications were not the primary driver of her thyrotoxicosis but was instead directly attributable to the HSCT.

In terms of prognosis, it is not clear whether this patient will follow the usual course in Graves’, in which there is around a 50% chance of going into remission after 12–18 months of antithyroid medications. In a retrospective study to monitor the outcome of 2ndADs over five years following HSCT, one case required ongoing treatment with carbimazole and another was treated with thyroidectomy (8).

This case highlights the importance of vigilant monitoring of thyroid functions in patients who receive HSCT and the challenges in managing such patients. Regarding this patient, the potential requirement for thyroidectomy in such a case where pharmacological management remains challenging must be an ongoing consideration for multidisciplinary teams. Early detection and timely intervention will help improve patient outcomes.
